content.title: Withdraw Decision
content.comment:
Dear PC, AC, and Reviewers,

We decide to withdraw our paper and submit it for the next venue.
Thanks to your constructive comments, we believe our paper becomes more clearer in this period.
Again, we really appreciate your service on meta-reviewing and reviewing on our paper.

Best Regards,

Authors.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a technique for dataset condensation: i.e., generating a set of synthetic exemplars that approximates the distribution of the original dataset. By doing so a smaller dataset can efficiently be used for repeated trainings (this is important in applications such continual learning). The prospered algorithm works by learning a set of codes (with a dimensionality smaller than the original data) for each class and a shared set of decoders that starting from the learnt codes produces synthetic exemplars. The optimization is done by minimizing the average representation (computed by random projections) between the real exemplars and the synthetic ones (averaged per class). Results show that the accuracy of the models trained with this technique is consistently better than other condensation algorithms in a variety of applications: normal training with different number of synthetic images per class, continual learning, and different architectures. For the presented experiments this algorithms also performs better than some generative models (e.g., VQVAE) at the same give number of parameters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The technique seems very effective and tackles an interesting problem.

Major Weaknesses (need to be address adequately to improve rating)
- Innovation compared to “Dataset Condensation with Distribution Matching” (DM) seems limited to avoiding subsampling codes, decoders and real data, the rest seems identical. This is ok since the current work brings attention to a very interesting phenomena given the difference in performance with and without sampling. However, I would have liked more discussion and investigation on this phenomena. For example, 
    - have the authors tried to replicate the DM results with their implementation when adding the sampling step? This would allow them to verify if the improvements they are observing is indeed all thanks to the sampling step or if there are other implementation details that might have played a fundamental role.
    - Another example:  The discussion at the end of page 5 seems to imply that g() is re-initialized every time? Is that the case? If so what happens when g() is not re-initialized? Why would re-initializing g() make sense? The authors left this as future work but given the limited novelty I think this is important to discuss in order to add value to the work.
- A few experiments decisions need justification or they might seem cherry picked (see next section for concrete examples)
- The results reported by these authors for KIP ConvNet do not seem to match the one reported in  the original paper “Dataset Distillation with Infinitely Wide Convolutional Networks. NeurIPS 2021.”. It is important to either explain why there is a mismatch or correct the table.

Minor Weaknesses (but important to address and correct them if accepted)
- A few statements are ambiguous, it would help to clarify them (see next section)
- The authors refer to eq (1) as MMD. This should be theoretically correct. However, it seems a trivial implementation of MMD that does not take advantage of the most powerful feature of such tool. MMD becomes powerful to compare distributions when using multiple momentum, additionally, by using a map that maps to a general reproducing kernel Hilbert space one can use the kernel trick to compute the discrepancy without knowing the exact function. In this case the authors are just computing the first momentum (mean) and the map is known (the randomly initialized network). Calling it MMD is not incorrect but it seems superfluous. Most reader will understand more easily that the authors are computing the L2 distance between average features. Unless it is possible to leverage all the power of MMD (which might lead to even better results).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is in general clear, however, the quality of the presentation could be improved. There are ambiguous statements that harm a bit the quality of the overall work and the ability to reproduce the experiments. Here are some concrete examples.
    - Often the authors talks about “parameter counts” but it seems to mean different things in different part of the text. For example  “we can dramatically increase the number of datapoints given a limited parameter count (e.g., the number of parameters used by synthetic images per each class)” clearly means that the parameter count is the overall size of the synthetic images. However a little bit later “even if the decoder is relatively large we can flexibly adjust the number of latent codes so that the total parameter counts are comparable.” Seems to imply that in the count one should also include the side of the decoders? or maybe of the codes? Or both?
    - Until very late in the paper it is hard to understand what the authors means by “knowledge sharing”. After reading it all I came to conclude that the knowledge sharing is related to the fact that decoders are shared (while the codes are per class). However I am still unsure. It would be great to explain this more explicitly.
    - For people that are not familiar with this field and the SOTA reading “X observed that what determines the performance of condensed dataset is its modality rather than resolution” is a bit cryptical. What does it mean here modality? This becomes clear only later. I would consider explaining what modality is.
	- “Intuitively, if we sample θ ∈ Θc, then each individual θ will try to explain the whole class set Xc at a time without considering the existence of other codes θ′ ∈ Θc\{θ} due to the sampling.” Isn’t this true 
also when simply comparing means as in the proposed algorithm? In Eq (1) there is nothing that forces the codes (or the decoders) to be different from each other. For example you could have a good disjoint set of codes that covers perfectly the desired space but their average could be bad. On the other hand, if all codes try to cover the whole distribution then their average will be better at minimizing eq (1) yet their representation of the distribution might be worse than the one provided by a disjoint set. This is connected to the fact that comparing only means might not tell the whole story and using also higher order might actually help.
	- In the “full batch training” the weights w_1 to w_k and their relation to the training step is not clear.
	- In table 1 the authors say “15 evaluations (3 training runs and 5 evaluations for each run).” Why would the evaluation run be different? Where is the stochasticity in the evaluation step?
	- In Figure 7: how is the |Bias| of the gradient computed?
- Some experimental choices need a bit of justification, for example:
    - Table 1: Why for CIFAR 100 and Tiny imagined the comparison is limited to 1 and 10 images while for SVHN and CIFAR 10 there is also a 50 images setting?
    - Figure 2: Why SVHN with 10 and 50 images (what about 1), but CIFAR 10 with 1 and 10 (what about 50)? 
    - On the comparison with generative model: how does the parameter count affect the number of images generated for the generative models? How many synthetic images were used for those experiments?
content.summary_of_the_review: While the work seems effective, the major weaknesses listed above are important to be resolved before this work can be published. If the authors can explain the weaknesses listed above adequately (especially the lack of novelty compared to “Dataset Condensation with Distribution Matching”) then I’d be happy to upgrade my rating to accept (but I would encourage the authors to address also the minor comments in order to improve the quality and the transparency with respect to reproducibility).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work aims to solve the dataset distillation problem by latent space knowledge factorization, which leverages an additional set of decoders to  
decode the distilled data. Inspired by the generative model, this paper leverages many decoders to decode the distilled data into different styles that are close to the augmented original data. Since the distilled data has fewer dimensions than the traditional distilled data,  the authors place more images per class (IPC) to compare with other baselines, which makes the comparison of the experiments unfair.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros
1. This paper is easy to follow.
2. Many distilled images are demonstrated in the figures. Besides, many kinds of experiments are presented in section 4. 
The derivation of Eq(2) in appendix C is good. 
Cons
1. The most significant problem of this paper is the unfair comparison. The information carried by the decoders has not been counted into the allowed information capacity. For example, ipc=10 on the cifar 10, then there should be a maximum of  $10 \times 3 \times 32 \times 32$ dimensions. However, the dimensions of the decoders are ignored, which are not included in the baselines. Moreover, the authors even put more samples to fill up the maximum of  $10 \times 3 \times 32 \times 32$, which makes the ipc=10 not correct on the proposed method. 
2. The first point of the cons explains why the improvement is more significant for the fewer IPC. Since the information carried by the decoders is fixed, fewer IPC will make the additional information more significant. Also, the authors should present the results of CIFAR-100 IPC=50. I am afraid the performance of ipc=50 on cifar-100 would be marginally improved or degraded. 
3. Can these decoders be used on different datasets? For example, a fixed batch of decoders can be generalized to MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet. The size of these decoders should be the same. Otherwise, they are a simple combination of the decoders on MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality of this paper is not guaranteed, as the comparison of experiments is unfair. The fair comparison should be the dimensions of the decoders should be included in the total $10 \times 3 \times 32 \times 32$, together with the distilled data. Each coordinate should be a float-16 number. That is a fair comparison. Otherwise, this paper compares their proposed method to different benchmarks. Because dataset distillation is also used for data storage, the saving size is the factor we need to control for a fair comparison. 


The novelty of this paper is limited. The inspiration of this paper for dataset distillation is modifying the evaluation metric of dataset distillation and changing the problem of dataset distillation into the encoder, decoder, or GAN problem, which is not significant to the community.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper is below the threshold of ICLR. The comparison of experiments is unfair, and the novelty of this paper is limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use very small decoders and a set of latent codes to parameterize synthetic images. The paper achieves good results on several benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, this paper is easy to follow and provides new results on this task.

Strengths:
+ The paper is well-written with clear structures and flow.
+ The results are good

Weakness:
- Two important works missing from the comparison while the paper mentions achieving significantly large margins on benchmarks. [1] and [2] are two recent works that achieve great results in Dataset Distillation. [1] proposes an approximated version of KIP that makes it scalable and easier to train. [2] also does re-parameterization and achieves better results on SVHN and CIFAR10. Both methods should be compared in table 1 and discussed in the paper in detail.

- The decoder structure on DD has been used and proposed in the previous literature, e.g. Zhao et al [3].

- Lack of principled contribution. Although the paper achieves good results, it seems to be simply combining the previous Distribution Matching learning objective with a small decoder structure (already tested in [3] on the DD task). Not many insights seem to be provided in this paper. 

- The parameterization methods seem to have scalability issues when applied to more advanced learning frameworks (e.g., the large number of synthetic examples)

- I'd encourage the authors to add a limitation section and discuss the potential limitations of the formulation/algorithm.

[1] Dataset Distillation using Neural Feature Regression
[2] Remember the Past: Distilling Datasets into Addressable Memories for Neural Networks
[3] Synthesizing Informative Training Samples with GAN

content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper misses critical comparisons with previous methods and lacks principled novelty. The main component is trying the combination of two existing parts in the community. The paper achieves good results.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new way of data parameterization in the dataset condensation problem. Instead of storing the raw images directly, the paper proposes to store some latent codes and some decoders. Images are generated by sending latent codes to decoders pair-wisely. In this case, we can use much less parameters to store more synthetic images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ The motivation to improve the efficiency of parameterization in dataset condensation is valid.
+ The derivations of the sampling bias (for synthetic datasets) and variance (for real datasets) can theoritically explain the drawback of mini-batch training used in a lot of previous methods. Nevertheless, the paper does not directly tackle this issue but simply adopts full-batch training. If the GPU runs out of memory, the method would compute the gradient for only a subset of synthetic dataset. I think it would be meaningful to explore more elegant ways in future works.
+ Experiments are also sufficient to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed parameterization.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are three major concerns:

- It is unclear that whether the proposed method would increase the burden of training using the synthetic dataset. Since there are significantly more images compared with the baseline, and each image has to be generated via a feed-forward decoder process in an online manner, the training time would also increase significantly. Given that one important target for the dataset condensation task is to alleviate the heavy training burden of deep neural networks, I think this is one fatal limitation for the proposed method.

- It is unclear that whether the proposed method "preserves quality of synthetic examples" as claimed. Although the authors provide the experimental results of using the same number of training iterations as the baseline, it is still hard to see whether it "preserves quality of synthetic examples", compared with conducting experiments under the same number of images.

- The proposed method is closely-related to generative modeling. Given that the proposed method does not care about the total number of images, in a special case of the proposed method, the latent vectors can be drawn from a random distribution, while the decoders can serve as generators, which is very similar to applying a generative model like GAN, VAE, and etc. In this view, the novelty of the method is somewhat limited. I know that the authors try to differentiate the proposed solution with these generative models in both related work and experiment sections. I believe that comparisons can be improved. Let's take GAN as an example. The gaps between the default form of the proposed method and GAN are actually two-fold:

  1. Use learnable latent codes or draw latent codes from a prior distribution.
  2. The training objective is DM-like or GAN-like.

  A more logical comparison should be making the changes step-by-step in an ablation study, rather than only comparing with BigGAN, which are unclear to readers where the performance gap comes from.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I think discussions on the following aspects are necessary:

* The training efficiency with the synthetic data compared with the original parameterization. Maybe wall-clock time is more proper as a metric compared with the number of iterations.
* Comparisons with the original parameterization under the condition of the same number of images are also expected.
* Proper comparisons with generative modeling.
* Data parameterization in dataset condensation is actually not a brand-new research topic recently. Although many works can be viewed as concurrent works, discussions on how the proposed method works different from them are expected, to bring more useful insights to the community of dataset condensation.

  [1] Remember the Past: Distilling Datasets into Addressable Memories for Neural Networks, Deng et al., NeurIPS 2022.

Based on the above analysis, I think that the preliminary rating of this paper should be at the borderline.

content.title: Dataset Condensation with Latent Space Knowledge Factorization and Sharing
content.TL;DR: We condense datasets by learning a set of learnable codes defined in a compact latent space followed by a set of tiny decoders which maps them differently to the original input space.
content.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for systematically solving dataset condensation problem in an efficient manner by exploiting the regularity in a given dataset. Instead of condensing the dataset directly in the original input space, we assume a generative process of the dataset with a set of learnable codes defined in a compact latent space followed by a set of tiny decoders which maps them differently to the original input space. By combining different codes and decoders interchangeably, we can dramatically increase the number of synthetic examples with essentially the same parameter count, because the latent space is much lower dimensional and since we can assume as many decoders as necessary to capture different styles represented in the dataset with negligible cost. Such knowledge factorization allows efficient sharing of information between synthetic examples in a systematic way, providing far better trade-off between compression ratio and quality of the generated examples. We experimentally show that our method achieves new state-of-the-art records by significant margins on various benchmark datasets, such as SVHN, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet.
